tldr: In humanoid whole-body control, aligning the intermediate features of a world action model predicting future visuals with VLM-generated language embeddings describing task progress and subsequent state changes significantly improves task success rates during training, without introducing any inference overhead.
hero_caption: Overview and performance of Language-Forcing. (a) Examples of whole-body tasks in simulation and on a real humanoid, along with language targets used exclusively during training. (b) Success rates outperforming existing methods, a fast inference latency of 91 ms, and feature attributions showing attention sharply focused on task-relevant objects.
overview:
Recently, World Action Models (WAMs)—which simultaneously learn robot action generation and future visual observation prediction—have attracted considerable attention. However, when relying solely on conventional visual prediction loss as a supervisory signal, models suffer from a fundamental issue: they disproportionately attend to scene-wide but task-irrelevant variations, such as camera viewpoint shifts or background motion, while neglecting visually subtle yet critical contact and state transitions, like the exact moment a hand touches a handle.

To tackle this, the authors asked: "Can we force intermediate visual prediction features using semantic information from language?" Specifically, pairs of current and short-horizon future frames are fed into a frozen, pre-trained Vision-Language Model (VLM) to generate descriptions of task progress—what has been achieved now and what will happen next. An auxiliary loss is then added to align these text embeddings with the intermediate future-visual features of the WAM.

Thanks to this design, the visual prediction representations stay focused on task-relevant objects and contact states without being distracted by background noise. Crucially, the auxiliary components like the VLM and text encoder are used only during training and can be pre-cached offline, introducing zero computational overhead or latency degradation during deployment on real robots.

Evaluated across seven tasks on the humanoid benchmark "HumanoidArena," Language-Forcing achieved an average success rate of 79.17%, outperforming the identical WAM baseline without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points and the strongest competing policy (GR00T N1.7) by 9.46 percentage points. Furthermore, on five real-world humanoid whole-body tasks, it significantly boosted the average success rate from 53.33% to 71.33%.
contributions: Proposed "Language-Forcing," a training strategy that evaluates task progress and subsequent states using a frozen VLM to align the future-visual features of a World Action Model (WAM) into a language space.
Maintained zero inference overhead by using the VLM and text encoder solely as auxiliary training components and caching their representations offline.
Achieved an average success rate of 79.17% on the whole-body humanoid benchmark "HumanoidArena," outperforming state-of-the-art baselines such as GR00T N1.7.
Demonstrated an 18.0 percentage point improvement in success rate (from 53.33% to 71.33%) over the baseline across five real-world humanoid loco-manipulation tasks via language alignment.

sections.heading: Why visual prediction alone falls short for humanoid whole-body control
sections.summary: While World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly predict actions and future observations are promising, they are easily distracted by large, irrelevant visual shifts like camera viewpoint motion, overlooking subtle contact changes. This paper proposes "Language-Forcing" to guide intermediate features using VLM-generated descriptions of task progress.
sections.details:
In humanoid loco-manipulation, coordinating base/torso posture and fine end-effector contacts is essential. Recently, World Action Models (WAMs) unifying action generation and future observation prediction have been widely studied, but they face a major pitfall.

Dense visual pixel prediction losses provide rich supervision, but they tend to overfit to large scene-wide visual shifts—such as background translation caused by camera movement—that are irrelevant to the task. Conversely, they downweight visually minor events that are critical for subsequent action decisions, such as the exact moment a finger contacts a doorknob. Furthermore, standard task prompts specify only the final goal ("open the door") and do not convey step-by-step progress along the transition.

To address this, the authors leverage the abstractive power of language. Textual descriptions like "grabbed the handle" or "the door opens next" explicitly capture what stage the robot is currently in and what should happen next. Having a VLM articulate this task progress and subsequent state changes, and aligning those language features with the WAM's internal future-visual features, forms the core intuition of Language-Forcing. Visual prediction models physical scene dynamics, while language supplies task-relevant semantic grounding.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of VLAs, world models, and humanoid whole-body control
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work across Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, world models, and humanoid whole-body control. Unlike previous approaches limited to static instructions or geometric alignment, this work injects temporal, transition-level progress language directly into future-visual representations.
sections.details:
This work is situated at the intersection of three major research areas:

### Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models and World Models
Robot policies leveraging large-scale demonstration datasets and pre-trained representations are advancing rapidly. In particular, continuous action generation using diffusion models or flow matching (such as $\pi_0$) and World Action Models (WAMs) incorporating future video prediction into action policies have emerged. However, studies have pointed out that improving visual prediction quality does not automatically translate into better closed-loop control.

### Whole-Body Humanoid Control Policies
Humanoid control has evolved beyond simple motion-capture imitation toward language-conditioned whole-body coordinated behaviors. Foundation models such as GR00T N1 and WholeBodyVLA, alongside evaluation platforms like HumanoidArena, have highlighted both the difficulty and importance of whole-body loco-manipulation coordinating legs, torso, arms, and hands.

### Language and Representation Learning for Policy Training
Prior research has explored using language for representation learning or reward design in robotics, as well as pre-aligning 3D geometric features (e.g., Spatial Forcing). Other works supervise WAM planning representations with event descriptions (e.g., WorldScape Policy 2.0). Language-Forcing distinguishes itself by isolating action-conditioned future-visual features and explicitly aligning them with verbalized task progress over short-horizon temporal transitions exclusively during training.

sections.heading: How Language-Forcing works: Sharpening features through the eyes of a VLM
sections.summary: The base WAM employs a DiT architecture with vision and action experts. During training only, a frozen VLM generates progress and next-state descriptions from current and future frame pairs, which are aligned via cosine similarity with the WAM's internal future-visual tokens using UMT5 embeddings. At inference time, these auxiliary branches are discarded, resulting in zero overhead.
sections.details:
Here is an overview of the architecture and workflow of Language-Forcing.

### 3.1 Preliminaries (Base Model Architecture)
The underlying WAM adopts an action-centric architecture based on GigaWorld-Policy 0.5. It processes four token groups using a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT): robot state tokens $S$, current image tokens $R$, noisy action tokens $U$, and future video latent tokens $F$. The attention mask design is crucial: future visual queries attend to all tokens ($S, R, U, F$), whereas action queries attend only to $S, R, U$. Consequently, the future video branch can be completely detached during inference when generating actions.

### 3.2 Motivation
A visual flow-matching loss alone cannot distinguish between large, inconsequential camera shakes and small, task-critical fingertip contacts. However, given a pair of current and future images, a VLM can readily perceive task progress—e.g., "the handle was grasped, so the door will open next." This semantic information is directly injected into the action-conditioned future visual tokens.

### 3.3 Concrete Pipeline of Language-Forcing
For each training sample, the current frame $I_t$ and a future frame $I_{t+48}$ at $\Delta = 0.96$ seconds (48 steps at 50 Hz) are placed side by side and fed into a frozen VLM (Gemma 4 12B). The VLM outputs text $y_t$ evaluating task progress and predicting the subsequent state. This text is encoded by a frozen text encoder (UMT5), yielding an average pooled vector $e_t \in \mathbb{R}^{4096}$ over non-padded tokens as the target.

Concurrently, future visual tokens $F_t^{(\ell)}$ are extracted from the $\ell$-th transformer block (block 22 in this paper) of the WAM backbone. After average pooling, they are mapped to the same 4096-dimensional space via a 2-layer MLP projector $P_\phi$. The cosine loss with respect to the target vector is computed as:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LF}} = 1 - \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \cos\left(P_{\phi}\left(\bar{F}_{b, t}^{(\ell)}\right), e_{b, t}\right)$$

The total training loss combines the base WAM loss (action flow loss + visual flow loss) and the language loss: $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAM}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{LF}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LF}}$ (with $\lambda_{\mathrm{LF}} = 1.0$).

### Practical Implementation Insights
VLM inference and text embedding generation are fully pre-computed (cached) offline before policy training begins. Thus, no heavy VLM execution runs inside the training loop, saving substantial compute. Furthermore, at inference time, both the language branch and the future video generation branch are completely omitted, incurring zero additional deployment latency.

(a) During training, progress targets generated by a frozen VLM and UMT5 are aligned with future-visual features from the 22nd layer of the MoT backbone. (b) During inference, the auxiliary language branch and future visual generation branch are decoupled, executing only the action expert with ultra-low latency.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Dramatic gains across simulation and real hardware
sections.summary: On 7 HumanoidArena tasks (240 trials × 7 = 1,680 trials), Language-Forcing achieved a top success rate of 79.17%. On 5 real-robot tasks, success jumped from 53.33% to 71.33%. Ablations confirm that verbalizing "progress and future predictions" rather than simple captions, along with strict temporal pairing between observations and text, is essential.
sections.details:
Extensive experiments were conducted in the simulation environment "HumanoidArena" and on real humanoid hardware.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations covered seven HumanoidArena tasks: soccer, desk-to-desk object transport, box placement, door opening, sofa sitting, boxing, and visual navigation. The evaluation protocol is rigorous: across standard environments and three out-of-distribution (OOD) settings—lighting shifts (visual), texture/obstacle modifications (semantic), and widened initial states (execution)—each task underwent 240 trials (1,680 trials in total).

### 4.2 Policy Performance (Simulation)
Language-Forcing achieved an average success rate of **79.17%** (Table 1). This outperforms the strongest baseline, GR00T N1.7 (69.70%), by 9.46 percentage points, and surpasses the identical WAM baseline without language alignment (68.39%) by 10.77 percentage points. Noticeable improvements were observed in tasks involving dynamic object contacts, such as soccer (87.08%) and desk transport (70.83%).

Visual feature attribution maps (Figure F3) reveal that while the baseline exhibits diffuse attention scattered across backgrounds, Language-Forcing sharpens attention onto task-relevant objects like the soccer ball, punch bag, and interacting end-effectors.

### 4.3 In-Depth Ablation Analysis
Ablations provide notable insights into why the method works:

- **Target Text Content (Figure F4 left)**: Aligning with simple descriptions of future frames (captions) achieved a 73.57% success rate, whereas verbalizing "task progress and subsequent state predictions" reached 79.17%. Contextualized progress is far more effective than static scene descriptions.
- **Temporal Alignment (Figure F4 right)**: When progress descriptions from other trajectories within the same task were shuffled and assigned randomly, the success rate dropped sharply to 63.21%. Accurate temporal correspondence with the ongoing transition is critical.
- **Data Efficiency**: Evaluating policies trained on 40%, 70%, and 100% of the demonstration data revealed that Language-Forcing trained on just 70% of the data (69.64%) outperformed the standard WAM trained on 100% (68.39%). In humanoid robotics where data collection is expensive, a 30% reduction in required demonstrations is a major advantage.
- **Alignment Layer and Loss Weight**: Performance peaked at transformer block 22 with weight $\lambda_{\mathrm{LF}} = 1.0$; placing alignment too close to output layers or setting an excessive weight (e.g., 2.0) degraded policy performance.

### 4.4 Real-World Experiments
On a physical humanoid robot, five tasks—box carrying, food preparation, visual navigation, clothes rack moving, and door opening—were evaluated across 30 trials each (Figure F5, Table 4). Language-Forcing boosted the average success rate from **53.33% to 71.33%** (+18.0 percentage points). On the multi-stage contact task "food preparation," success jumped from 30.00% to 56.67% (+26.67 percentage points). Furthermore, inference latency remained at a practical 91 ms on an RTX 4090, well within the requirements for real-time control.

captions.F3: Visual feature attribution maps. Under Language-Forcing (w/ LF), attention is sharply focused on task-relevant elements such as the soccer ball, punching bag, grasping hands, and target objects, whereas the baseline (w/o LF) shows attention diffusely scattered across the background.
captions.F4: Ablations on language supervision design. The left panel shows that phrasing targets as task progress and future state changes yields the highest success rate (79.17%). The right panel demonstrates that shuffling the text targets degrades performance severely, underscoring the necessity of strict temporal pairing with observations.
captions.F5: Five real-world whole-body loco-manipulation tasks evaluated on a physical humanoid: (1) visual navigation, (2) box carrying, (3) door opening, (4) food preparation, and (5) clothes rack moving. Language-Forcing achieved significantly higher success rates than the baseline across all tasks.

sections.heading: Takeaway: Infusing predictive representations with task context through language
sections.summary: Language-Forcing is an effective training strategy that uses VLM-driven progress evaluation and semantic alignment to focus WAM future-visual features on task-critical transitions. It provides a practical blueprint for boosting humanoid whole-body control without incurring inference costs.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates an effective synergy between physical world modeling via visual prediction and abstract task understanding via language models.

Subtle contacts and transitions that are easily lost in pure pixel-level predictions are brought to the forefront through the descriptions of a powerful VLM observer. By distilling this understanding into intermediate feature representations solely during training, the policy network remains lightweight and fast during deployment—an appealing design for resource-constrained robotic systems.

Rigorous stress-testing in simulation and diverse real-world task completions substantiate the generalizability and robustness of Language-Forcing. It represents a compelling candidate to become a standard training technique for humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation and world-model-based policy learning.

sections.heading: Appendix: Training configurations and inference optimization details
sections.summary: The appendix details the HumanoidArena dataset composition (1,400 episodes total), definitions of the four evaluation modes, and key-value (KV) caching and quantization techniques achieving 91 ms inference latency on an RTX 4090.
sections.details:
The paper's appendix provides key technical details essential for reproducibility and real-world deployment:

- **Dataset Configuration**: Across the 7 HumanoidArena tasks, a total of 1,400 episodes (100 SONIC and 100 TWIST2 episodes per task) were used, comprising approximately 856k frames and 788k 48-step training windows. All policies were trained under an identical 50k-step budget and evaluated using EMA (Exponential Moving Average) checkpoints.
- **Evaluation Randomization Criteria**: In addition to standard evaluation, policies were challenged by three OOD settings: Visual mode (randomizing lighting direction, intensity, and RGB color), Execution mode (expanding initial state distributions, e.g., soccer ball lateral placement widened from [-1.2, 1.2] to [-1.45, 1.45]), and Semantic mode (replacing the punching bag with a box, adding distractor objects, etc.).
- **Real-Robot Inference Optimization**: During real-robot deployment, combining attention Key-Value (KV) caching with quantization techniques achieved an inference latency of 91 ms on a single RTX 4090 (24GB). This low latency supports closed-loop control without compromising whole-body dynamic stability.

takeaways: Because visual prediction losses can be swayed by dominant background shifts, aligning intermediate features with VLM descriptions of task progress and subsequent state changes is remarkably effective.
Supervisory language must express transition progress within the task context rather than generic image captions, and it must strictly match the observation temporally.
VLM inference and text embeddings can be pre-computed offline, and the language branch is detached during inference, preserving real-time execution speeds.
Language-Forcing exhibits high data efficiency, matching or exceeding full-dataset baseline performance using approximately 30% fewer demonstration trajectories.
limitations: An offline preprocessing pipeline is required prior to policy training to run VLM inference and generate text embeddings across the entire dataset.

Performance can be sensitive to the choice of the alignment layer (block 22 in this paper) and the loss weight ($\lambda=1.0$), potentially requiring hyperparameter tuning for different model backbones.
The approach depends on the VLM's (Gemma 4 12B) capacity to resolve task progress from given camera angles and resolutions, which may limit effectiveness in heavily occluded contact scenarios.
